Nov 4 : Chinese genetic sequencing firm Novogene sued the Pentagon late Tuesday in U.S. District Court in Washington over its inclusion on a US list of companies allegedly aiding Beijing's military. In June, the Defense Department added Novogene, Chinese e-commerce giant Alibaba internet search provider Baidu and automakers BYD and NIO and others to its list of "Chinese military companies" that prohibits the Defense Department from contracting directly with the firms. A number of Chinese firms have sued the Pentagon over the designations.

BRUGES, Belgium, Nov 4 : Hackers who cranked up fridge temperatures at supermarkets across Europe may have gained access through public internet-connected systems protected by default passwords or outdated software, a cybersecurity expert said. The second cyberattack in three weeks hit fridge systems at supermarket chains including Carrefour and Delhaize in Belgium, and ICA and Coop in Sweden, forcing retailers to discard spoiled food and raising concerns about food security. Three blood banks in France were also hit. Authorities have not publicly disclosed how the attackers gained access, and no perpetrator has been identified. Laurens Singier, an ethical hacker and researcher at Cyber 3 Lab, part of Howest University of Applied Sciences in Bruges, Belgium, said internet-connected systems which can be accessible remotely often have weak protections.

"In this case, the weak point was mainly putting those devices on the public internet. They shouldn't even be there," he said, speaking from a lab full of servers and systems similar to those that could control supermarket store fridges. A common problem with such systems is that operators fail to change default passwords set by the manufacturer, while others run older software with known vulnerabilities, he said. AI was now making it easier for amateurs to pull off hacks, Singier added. Supermarkets on Tuesday said they had taken hacked fridges offline, in line with guidance from refrigeration monitoring software provider Danfoss, whose systems were again among those targeted. Danfoss has said it is working with clients on fixes. Singier said that retailers should check they understand how they connect to the store interface, strengthen passwords, and consider switching from internet-based systems to more secure systems using SIM cards, like those used by solar panels and car chargers. "After this attack, we've seen a lot less of these devices publicly on the internet," he said. "But if you look at the numbers, there's still a lot of industrial devices which are open to the public, and in a lot of cases you yourself as the butcher or the chocolatier don't even know about it."

Source: Reuters

WASHINGTON, Nov 4 : Prediction markets got the big picture right in the US midterm elections, although a few races delivered surprises as Democrats seized control of the Senate and House of Representatives. With more than $1.48 billion wagered on Tuesday's elections, the results offered a test of whether prediction markets could translate their odds into accurate electoral forecasts. Bets placed on a Democratic midterm sweep largely paid off despite some mispriced races, as tens of millions of voters delivered a stinging rebuke to US President Donald Trump. "Prediction markets priced the midterm outcome within hours," said Kelly Ye, head of research at digital asset trading platform Talos.

Several closely contested Senate races had attracted millions of dollars in bets, putting prediction markets under scrutiny. In many cases, the results tracked expectations, with Democrats winning Senate seats in Texas and Ohio. "This was the first true prediction markets election," said Harry Crane, professor of statistics at Rutgers University. "The markets projected Democratic wins across the board throughout the closing weeks of the campaign, and were quick to react in real time to voting information as it rolled in," he added. Prediction markets rose to prominence as they diverged from traditional opinion polls by signaling a Trump victory in 2024, and analysts were scrutinizing their performance this week. While the markets cite high accuracy rates in their betting odds, some high-profile misses during the US primaries and in Brazil's presidential election have shown they are fallible. Prediction markets allow users to buy and sell contracts tied to real-world events, with prices reflecting traders' collective expectations. Critics, however, say those odds can be skewed by speculation, thin liquidity and concentrated bets. Kalshi's total trading volume on election markets reached over $2.5 billion this cycle, compared with $1.3 billion during the 2024 election cycle, which included the presidential race. Traders on Kalshi were assigning a 55 per cent probability to a "blue tsunami" as early as April. Meanwhile, Polymarket's election forecasts were about 98 per cent accurate, a person familiar with the matter told Reuters. One notable miss came in conservative South Carolina, where Democrat Annie Andrews defeated Republican Darline Graham to win a Senate seat, defying market expectations. Kalshi and Polymarket had implied a 70 per cent chance of Graham, the sister of the late US Senator Lindsey Graham, winning that race as of late afternoon Tuesday. "Prediction markets can be useful because they aggregate the views of people who have an incentive to be right, not just to express an opinion," said Brian Jacobsen, chief economic strategist at Annex Wealth Management. "They can give a good indication of where the weight of information is pointing, but a prediction isn't a promise. Whether it’s politics or sports, you still have to hold the election or play the game to know the result," he added.

Source: Reuters

Nov 4 : Data-center developer TeraWulf said on Wednesday it has secured a credit backstop agreement with Alphabet's Google to support financing needs for its data-center project with Claude creator Anthropic. The company also announced an expanded agreement with construction and engineering firm Fluor Enterprises for the development of the data-center site in Hawesville, Kentucky. The credit agreement with Google is the latest example of how major tech firms are providing multi-billion-dollar financial backstops and guarantees to help smaller AI companies, including neoclouds and data-center developers, fund the costly AI infrastructure build-out. TeraWulf had in July signed a 20-year lease with Anthropic for data-center infrastructure. The deal is expected to generate about $19 billion in contracted revenue for TeraWulf, which is among a group of companies that are shifting from bitcoin mining to providing critical AI infrastructure amid booming demand.

PARIS, Nov 4 : French cooperative bank Credit Mutuel Arkea said on Wednesday it had been hit by a cyberattack which "enabled fraudulent transactions to be carried out" but that clients' money was not affected. The bank said in a statement that the amount of money affected by the attack is still being assessed but is "not of a nature to undermine the Group’s financial strength and soundness." It did not give further details about the fraudulent transactions. The incident has been contained, operations are resuming, and client assets are not affected, Credit Mutuel Arkea said. The group told the relevant authorities as soon as the attack was detected, it added. Credit Mutuel Arkea is made up of Credit Mutuel's federations in Brittany and the southwest of France, as well as affiliated local banks and about 40 subsidiaries. The bank has 5.8 million clients and €211.5 billion ($237.51 billion) in assets, making it a major French financial firm, although significantly smaller than the likes of BNP Paribas and Societe Generale.

Nov 4 : Qualcomm has signed a multi-year agreement with SpaceX to supply radio equipment, baseband units and software for Starlink Mobile's planned nationwide terrestrial 5G network, as the Elon Musk-led space company seeks to challenge established US wireless carriers. The equipment will be deployed across tens of thousands of macro cell sites in the country starting in 2027, Qualcomm said on Wednesday. While the company did not disclose the financial terms of the agreement, it said "this is our biggest 5G deal yet." The deal will expand the presence of Qualcomm, best known for the chips that power smartphones, in the telecom infrastructure market, where it will compete with Marvell, Broadcom and Intel by supplying chips used in cell tower gear. Qualcomm, which has been seeking to diversify beyond mobile devices, already helps power 5G networks in Japan and Vietnam.

SpaceX aims to establish a major nationwide US wireless carrier, taking on incumbents AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile through a combination of satellite connectivity and terrestrial network. Although questions remain about the feasibility of SpaceX's plans, given the substantial investment required to compete with the Big Three, the company has been moving ahead with spectrum acquisitions and exploring deals with cell tower firms to expand its terrestrial network. Qualcomm said the equipment would provide a flexible foundation for a multi-band network, which can be deployed in stages. The initial rollout will focus on terrestrial 5G, with the architecture designed to accommodate developments in connectivity and network intelligence. The company's radio technology is designed to improve coverage, capacity and spectral efficiency, or the amount of data that can be transmitted over a given amount of spectrum. Advanced beamforming technology will help direct wireless signals toward users, allowing SpaceX to make more efficient use of its licensed spectrum.

BENGALURU, Nov 4 - India's cybercrime agency has warned banks, non-bank lenders and other financial firms of cyberattacks carried out with the help of artificial intelligence agents, amid a surge in incidents targeting the sector. "These attacks are financially motivated and are being carried out with the help of Artificial Intelligence (AI) agents leading to machine speed compromise," the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C) said in an advisory made public on Wednesday.  The warning comes at a time when regulators around the world, including those in the US and Britain, are stepping up efforts to contain AI risks. Last month, AI models under test broke into Indian organisations' live systems and read confidential records undetected, in the country's first such official account after similar incidents of rogue AI behaviour worldwide.

India has also seen a surge in cyber incidents in recent weeks. Data of 3,900 customers was leaked at State Bank of India, the country's largest lender. The Reserve Bank of India has also warned banks of rising cyberattacks on financial infrastructure, seeking proof of compliance with existing rules and details of their preparedness for AI-related risks, Reuters reported last week. The cybercrime agency said hackers exploit unpatched software or misconfigured IT systems to compromise infrastructure, then target automated fund disbursement systems or application programming interfaces (APIs) used for payments and fund transfers. The use of an agentic AI framework makes it possible to carry out such attacks at machine speed, it added. The I4C asked all financial entities, including banks, fintech firms and payment aggregators, to implement measures outlined by CERT-In, the government's cybersecurity agency, on October 9. It also suggested additional safeguards, such as setting daily and per-transaction limits, verifying beneficiary names and watching for unusual transaction speeds.

Nov 4 : The rise of AI-led shopping is posing a conundrum for retailers like Walmart and Amazon: how to enable AI agents to shop on their websites, without threatening their lucrative advertising revenue and the customer data that fuels it. Retail powerhouses Walmart and Amazon are also the world's two largest retail media businesses, dominating the estimated $74.4 billion in US retail media spending with a combined 88 per cent share of that market, according to projections from data firm Emarketer. But digital assistants could soon disrupt that business. AI-powered agents that can research and purchase products on consumers' behalf — like Meta's recently released Muse — could erode the highly profitable business of brands paying retailers to promote products on their websites and apps. Morgan Stanley researchers said in July these agents could account for 10 per cent to 20 per cent of US e-commerce spending by 2030. Amazon and Walmart are taking different approaches to agentic AI shopping. Amazon has blocked Muse, while Walmart is officially partnering with Meta's agentic tool.

So far, there is no meaningful effect yet on Amazon ads from third-party agents, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said last week. However, the company's 11 per cent year-over-year growth in advertising revenue for the third quarter was its slowest pace of growth in nearly four years, LSEG data show. The segment consistently accounts for about 10 per cent of total net sales. DIFFERENT APPROACHES Amazon banned Muse from its website in September, saying it appeared to have accessed its online store without authorization, capturing and storing customer credentials. Meta declined to comment. The e-commerce leader told Reuters this week that third-party agents should operate openly and respect service providers' decisions about whether or not to participate. Amazon also won a court order blocking Perplexity's shopping agent Comet in March, though the 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals overturned the ban in August, a decision Amazon said it disagreed with. The case is ongoing. Walmart, conversely, rolled out infrastructure on October 21 to enable third-party agentic commerce. When a shopper uses an agent to browse, Walmart will create a profile for that agent that links to the shopper's Walmart account. Consumers can approve purchases or set spending limits. Walmart CFO John David Rainey told analysts and investors in August that advertising, which includes the Walmart Connect retail media business, along with its membership and marketplace operations, accounted for 45 per cent of quarterly operating income growth. Walmart does not separately break out Walmart Connect's figures in its earnings release. Dan Marc, CEO of retail media platform Footprints AI, said he expects companies like Amazon and Walmart to start signing their largest advertisers to multiyear ad deals to secure those revenues, and also expects more discounts on digital retail media ads as shoppers turn to large language models and agentic tools. Walmart declined to comment. SHIFTING MARKETING LANDSCAPE Morningstar analyst Brett Husslein said the moment presents "an evolution rather than an existential threat" for retail media. Brands are expected to spend 22.6 per cent more on retail media in 2026 than last year's $60.7 billion, Emarketer forecasts show. This year, Walmart started testing ads within Sparky, its AI shopping chatbot, just as Amazon has embedded them in its AI shopping assistant, Alexa for Shopping. Advertising for bots may rely less on visual flair or emotional resonance and more on specific product data that matches customer queries using AI chatbots, industry practitioners and consultants say. Companies including Procter & Gamble, Nestle and L'Oreal have said they are trying to make product information digestible for AI agents. Those agents are bringing brands closer to consumers, said Mondelez's vice president of global digital commerce, Andrew Lederman, on a podcast in April. He said retailer media sites currently still drive the vast majority of volume for the company. "We are not recommending that clients fundamentally shift their retail media budgets overnight," said Amie Owen, chief client officer at digital commerce consultancy Flywheel. "But we are advising them to prepare for how discovery and purchase decisions may evolve." Katherine Black, a senior consultant at Kearney, envisions a radical shift, in which retail media eventually evolves into a kind of "bidding system" where agents search for a product at a consumer’s price point, and retailers set price ceilings and floors. "All retailers need to be thinking about how to interact with consumers in new ways," Black said.

Source: Reuters

Nov 4 : Solstice Advanced Materials raised its 2026 forecasts on Wednesday after strong demand from data centers for its nuclear, refrigerant and electronic materials and higher prices helped it surpass third-quarter estimates. Surging investment in AI infrastructure and more complex chips are boosting demand for the specialty material maker's products used in cooling systems, high-performance computing and nuclear power generation. Sales of electronic materials rose over 31 per cent to $135 million in the third quarter. Refrigerant sales increased 8.3 per cent to $433 million, supported by automotive and data center cooling applications, while backlog in its nuclear business is now at $2.6 billion. CEO David Sewell told Reuters that although geopolitical tensions have increased the cost of diesel and sulfur, the impact on Solstice remained immaterial given its limited exposure to the Middle East and its ability to hike prices.

Nov 4 : Data center stocks slid on Wednesday, while clean-energy shares rallied after Democrats seized control of Congress, prompting investors to reposition for tougher scrutiny of the AI boom and a shift in policy priorities. The Democratic sweep, which included victories in traditional Republican strongholds and key data-center hubs Texas and Georgia, will usher in divided government in Washington and raises the prospect of greater congressional oversight of industries that benefited from Republican control. Market reaction rippled across AI-linked stocks, renewables, healthcare companies, defense contractors and prison operators. DATA CENTER AND UTILITY STOCKS

Data center operators lost ground, with Applied Digital and CoreWeave down 4.1 per cent and 5.3 per cent, respectively. Cipher Digital slid 14.3 per cent. The data center boom sparked public backlash this year, raising concerns that tighter Democratic oversight could slow investment just as investors grow wary of soaring AI spending and uncertain returns. Though analysts doubt any legislation could meaningfully stall data center construction, a Democratic-led Congress increases prospects of more hearings and investigations related to the AI buildout. "AI has been an enormous engine powering the US economy, so any curbs on its future development could threaten to put the brakes on growth," said Kit Rees, investment strategist at Quilter. Utilities and equipment suppliers exposed to the data-center boom also came under pressure. GE Vernova fell 5.8 per cent, while Constellation Energy and Vistra, among the power companies most exposed to data-center projects in Texas, slid 5 per cent and 9 per cent, respectively. CLEAN ENERGY A Democratic sweep could bolster expectations for continued federal support for clean energy while speeding approvals for energy and infrastructure projects. Democrats plan to scrutinize the Trump administration's efforts to roll back emissions rules and could use the Congressional Review Act to overturn regulations that make it easier to sell gas-powered trucks and SUVs. Shares of solar maker First Solar gained 13.8 per cent, residential solar installer Sunrun added 12.5 per cent and inverter maker Enphase Energy was up 10.2 per cent. Clean-power developer NextEra Energy inched 3.7 per cent higher. "The more that oil and gas prices rise, the bigger the incentive, the bigger the economic incentive to roll out clean energy," said Paul Jackson, global market strategist for EMEA at Invesco. Europe's Vestas and Orsted rose 2.9 per cent and 4.7 per cent, respectively, while Portugal's EDP Renewables was up 2.3 per cent. ELON MUSK-LED COMPANIES Shares of Elon Musk's rocket and space technology company SpaceX dropped 4.6 per cent to its lowest since mid-August, while EV maker Tesla was down 5.7 per cent. "It puts into doubt a potential merger between SpaceX and Tesla. While Congress cannot stop a merger, they could slow it down via extra scrutiny," said Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB. "Musk had poured hundreds of millions into the Republican Party ahead of these elections...we could see stocks linked to Musk struggle now that his political enemies have won back control of Congress." Trump Media & Technology Group, majority-owned by Trump, dropped 7 per cent. DEFENSE STOCKS Defense contractors such as Northrop Grumman fell 2.7 per cent, while RTX, Lockheed Martin and L3Harris lost between 2 per cent and 4 per cent each. The sector had been underpinned by expectations that the $1.5-trillion budget request by Trump would not face headwinds in a Republican-dominated Congress. However, analysts expect the funding to fall short of expectations under a Democratic-led Congress. "A difficult debt ceiling negotiation could delay the spending increases, leaving companies that rely on new government contracts more exposed than those with established ones," said Lale Akoner, global market strategist at etoro. "The real risk is that spending rises more slowly than anticipated, which will lead to price corrections." HEALTH INSURERS AND HOSPITAL OPERATORS Shares of hospital operators such as HCA Healthcare and Universal Health Services gained 7.2 per cent and 5.9 per cent, respectively. Insurers such as Centene rose 4.8 per cent and Molina was up 6.4 per cent. Democrats have pushed for universal healthcare policies that could mean more government spending allocated to the sector. "The outcome would give Congress greater latitude to pursue Democratic healthcare priorities, including reinstating enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies or reversing elements of the GOP's Medicaid cuts, such as work requirements," Morgan Stanley analysts write in a note. "Although we continue to view meaningful healthcare policy changes as unlikely before the next presidential election cycle, the results could shift the policy narrative." PRISON OPERATORS Prison operators such as GEO Group and CoreCivic fell 7 per cent and 4.8 per cent, respectively. The two stocks have rallied sharply since Trump won the presidency two years ago, as his clampdown on illegal immigration boosted the need for detention facilities.

Source: Reuters

Nov 4 : Advanced Micro Devices rose 3 per cent in early trading after the US chipmaker forecast faster growth through 2027, reassuring investors that demand for AI infrastructure remains strong. The company's strong outlook highlighted growing momentum in its server processor business, signaling that spending on AI computing was extending beyond Nvidia's accelerators, which dominate the market. "We see demand across the data-center business, across our CPU business, as well as our data-center AI business," CEO Lisa Su said, adding the company had been preparing for that growth for several years. Su said on Tuesday that the company expects overall revenue to rise more than 80 per cent in 2027, which is higher than the 77 per cent growth analysts estimate, according to LSEG data.

Nov 4 : German defence AI firm Helsing said on Wednesday it had handed Germany's military procurement agency the source code for a mission operating system intended for future combat drones and other air warfare systems, giving the government ownership of software that has traditionally remained in industry hands. Known as MissionOSBw, the software is a key part of Germany's Combat Fighter System of Systems Nucleus (CFSN) programme, approved by the parliament in July.  Worth about €580 million ($651 million), according to industry documents previously reported by Politico, the project includes two experimental uncrewed combat aircraft, ground control stations, autonomy software and a government-owned reference architecture. It is being developed by a consortium led by Helsing alongside Hensoldt, Rohde & Schwarz, MBDA and Diehl Defence. Helsing said it had transferred the source code, documentation and software development kit to procurement agency BAAINBw, with ownership of the software remaining with the German state.

The arrangement is unusual in a defence industry where prime contractors often retain control over key software, interfaces and intellectual property. The software is designed to allow modules from different suppliers to be added, upgraded or replaced independently, reducing reliance on a single contractor. Helsing said it followed the Modular Open Systems Approach, a model intended to speed up upgrades and simplify integration of new capabilities. The emphasis on state ownership comes after years of disputes over industrial control in Europe's future combat-air programmes. The fighter element of European FCAS air defence programme had become mired in clashes between Dassault Aviation and Airbus Defence and Space over leadership and share of work, while CFSN is built around software owned by the German state rather than any individual contractor.
